analysis.one_liner: Bars FDA tobacco regulation while tying federal health grants to state youth-smoking laws.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Commerce Committee without ever getting a vote or a hearing-documented action, and none of its provisions became law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would do two opposite things at once. It would permanently declare that the Secretary of Health and Human Services has no power to regulate how cigarettes are made, labeled, sold, or advertised — shutting the door on the FDA, which at the time was moving to regulate tobacco. In exchange, it would require every state to pass a list of youth-access laws (minimum age 18 with photo ID, no single-cigarette sales, vending machine and billboard limits, retailer licensing) or lose up to 20% of its federal preventive health block grant, with penalties for noncompliance climbing to 80%. The bill never got a vote; it sat in committee until the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, teenagers would have faced harder paths to buying cigarettes: photo-ID age checks, bans on single 'loosie' sales, supervised vending machines and self-service displays, no free samples by mail, and no tobacco billboards within sight of schools or playgrounds. Tobacco manufacturers would also have benefited enormously, because the bill would have written into law that no federal agency can regulate their product's manufacture, labeling, sale, or advertising.

how_it_helps.text: States would have to make it illegal to sell tobacco to anyone under 18, with buyers required to show photo identification, and illegal for minors to buy or use fake ID, backed by fines, community service, and education programs.
It would ban sales of single cigarettes and packs of fewer than 20 — the cheap formats most accessible to kids with little money.

Vending machines and self-service displays would have to be supervised or restricted, free samples and mail-order sales to minors would be banned, and retailers would need a state license and would face annual unannounced inspections.
Tobacco billboards could not be placed in view of schools or playgrounds, and cigarette brand names and logos could not be put on items marketed to children, such as toys and video games.

States that failed to enact or enforce these laws would lose a growing share of their federal preventive-health block grants — 20% rising to 80% for repeated noncompliance — and grant money could be spent on enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would give up nothing they valued more than FDA jurisdiction: the bill's first section hands them a permanent statutory shield from federal regulation of their manufacturing, labeling, sale, and advertising. Retailers would bear licensing, inspection, and signage costs. Minors themselves would face fines of up to $100 for buying and $250 for using fake ID, plus community service. The public would bear the opportunity cost: the bill would foreclose stronger federal regulation, such as FDA oversight of cigarette design and marketing, in exchange for a state-by-state enforcement scheme.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retailers, minors fined — while tobacco makers gain FDA immunity

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip the Secretary of Health and Human Services of any authority to regulate the manufacture, labeling, sale, distribution, advertising, and promotion of tobacco under existing federal law — permanently closing the door on the stricter FDA regulation that was under consideration at the time.
It punishes the young buyers themselves — fines, community service, and mandatory education — rather than focusing penalties on manufacturers or the supply chain.

Its public-health teeth depend entirely on states choosing to act: a state unwilling to pass the required laws would simply lose block grant money, and the bill sets no federal enforcement of its own.

The penalties on retailers are modest — for example, an owner who fails to notify clerks about the law faces a fine of only $100 to $250 — and the licensing fee structure is left entirely to each state.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The youth-access measures had real value: age checks, bans on single-cigarette sales, and supervised vending machines are exactly the tools later public-health campaigns used to cut teen smoking. But the price was steep and structural — writing FDA authority out of tobacco law permanently, at the very moment the FDA was preparing stricter rules covering advertising and cigarette design. An honest reading is that the bill traded a strong federal option for a weaker, state-dependent one, and its decision to fine teenagers for buying rather than penalizing the industry limits how much of the gain went to the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee in October 1995, and it never came out — no markup, no floor vote — before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Scotty Baesler, a Democrat from tobacco-growing Kentucky, introduced the bill on September 28, 1995, with three Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced, and on October 13, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

The bill's central structural provision was a declaration that the Secretary of Health and Human Services has no authority to regulate tobacco manufacture, labeling, sale, distribution, advertising, or promotion under existing federal statutes, with regulation instead conditioned on state block grants.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a change in law, because nothing happened. But because the bill died, tobacco manufacturers never got the statutory immunity from FDA regulation it would have written into law, and the FDA's separate push to regulate tobacco remained unblocked — a question settled later in the courts and, eventually, by a 2009 law giving the FDA real tobacco authority.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — no FDA shield for tobacco makers

for.name: Rep. Scotty Baesler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Youth Smoking Prevention Act on September 28, 1995.

for.name: 3 of 204 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors are recorded.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 28, 1995, and referred it to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment on October 13; never reported it out or scheduled any action.

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill before the Congress ended; Bliley, whose Virginia district was tobacco country, presided over a committee that sat on tobacco-regulation measures in this period.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists; its sponsor and all three recorded cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-run committee it died in took no recorded action either way.

industries.note: The bill's first section would permanently declare that no federal health agency can regulate how cigarettes are made, labeled, sold, or advertised — locking in the industry's freedom from FDA oversight even as it accepts state youth-access rules. Had it passed, tobacco makers would have gained a statutory shield just as the FDA was preparing stricter regulation.

industries.industry: Tobacco retailers and vending machine operators
industries.note: Retailers would face state licensing, annual unannounced inspections, bans on single-cigarette sales, and supervised displays and vending machines. Their business model of selling loose cigarettes and unsupervised access to minors is exactly what the bill targets.
Tobacco billboards could no longer be placed within sight of schools or playgrounds, cutting revenue from a category of ad space that depended on visibility near places children gather.

States would get federal grant money they could use to enforce youth-tobacco laws, but would lose 20% of preventive-health block grants — rising to 80% for repeated noncompliance — if they failed to pass or follow the required laws.
Tobacco brand names and logos could not appear on items marketed specifically to minors, eliminating a niche of paid brand placements.
